info.description:
What another system needs from the DMS, and nothing else. Three ways in:

* **An application** - its own key (`X-DMS-Api-Key`, or `Authorization: Bearer`). The key names what it may
  read and **the AD account it acts as**: the DMS answers exactly what that account may see.
* **The company's AI** - a ticket minted for the person who asked (`/api/ai/index-ticket`). The answer is
  then what *that person* may read, file by file. The ticket does not say whose it is and cannot be pointed
  at somebody else.
* **A page of the repository** - a dashboard or a KPI page runs sandboxed and cannot sign in, so it is given
  a page key when it is opened (`?t=`), good for its own folder and for a few hours. Reading only.

Nothing here stands in for a right the person or the account does not have. One endpoint writes (the KPI
Builder's); the rest read.

Guides: `docs/09-Machine-API.md` (applications and the AI), `docs/08-KPI-Builder-Contract.md` (the KPI
Builder), `docs/07-KPI-Integration.md` (the page key). The DMS page's own endpoints are not here: they are
in `docs/10-Swagger.md`, and in `/api/openapi-all.json` for a client that really wants them.
info.title: RH DMS - the API other systems use

get.description:
A ticket the company's AI uses to index what this person may read, just before it answers them.

The RAG is given it by the page when the person asks AI Insights, and calls
/api/v1/approved-documents with it. Everything it gets back is filtered by that person's own AD
rights, file by file - an application key names a service account and would answer the same list to
everybody, which is exactly what must not happen here.

A file of that folder as data a page can draw: a workbook as its sheets and rows, a JSON as what
it says, anything else as its text. A browser cannot open an .xlsx by itself and the server may have
no way out to fetch a library for it - the DMS reads workbooks anyway, for the AI.
tags: Pages of the repository (the page key)

post.description:
Where to send this person to make a KPI, or to change one. The page asks for this rather than
building the address itself: the folder is checked here - that it is a KPIs folder of the skeleton,
and that this person may add to it - so a folder named in a browser grants nothing (DMS-005).
tags: Pages of the repository (the page key)

get.description:
Can a page reach the DMS at all? This one answers without a key and without a sign-in, so it says
which of the two is in the way: open it in the browser (/api/kpi/ping). A sign-in prompt or 401 means
IIS is still asking for one on /api/kpi (scripts/Set-DmsKpiKeyAccess.ps1); an answer means the way is
open and anything still failing is the key or the address.
tags: Pages of the repository (the page key)

get.description:
The Markdown of every approved document, as it lies in the Current_ReadOnly folders.

Four things per file: the document's id, its name, its revision and where the Markdown is. This is
the AI's list - it reads these files - so it is taken from the folders themselves and not only from
the register: a document released by hand is in Current_ReadOnly with its Markdown beside it, and the
AI should read that too. What the register knows fills in the id and the revision; what it does not
know is read from the Markdown's own first lines, which the DMS wrote when it made the file.

get.description:
Every approved document the DMS holds, with the file that is in force and the Markdown beside it.

This is what the company's AI reads from: it asks the DMS which documents are approved and where
their files are, instead of being pointed at a folder and left to guess what in it is current. A
revision that has been replaced is not here; nor is anything still in work.

One released file, served by the DMS itself - the content, not a path on the file server.

This is how the company's AI reads a document without an account on the file server: it asks for the
file, and the DMS answers only if the AD account behind the call may see it - the key's own account,
or, with a ticket, the person who asked. Only what is released (Current_ReadOnly) is served, so an
index built from this holds the revisions in force and nothing in work.

post.description:
The KPI Builder publishes one KPI of one department: its page and the data behind it, together.

    POST /api/v1/kpi/publish   department=Production  kpi=Yield
                               files=@Yield.html  files=@Yield.json

What it makes, under that department's KPIs folder:

    KPIs\Yield\Yield.html                      the page, writable - the next build replaces it
    KPIs\Yield\Current_ReadOnly\Yield.json    the data, released: read only, in the register

One KPI, one folder named after it, made on the first publish - and the KPIs folder itself made if
the department has none yet. A page named dashboard_<something>.html is the department's dashboard
rather than one KPI: it stays at the root of KPIs and its data is released into the KPIs folder's
own Current_ReadOnly, which is where a dashboard layout belongs.

The application acts as its AD account: that account needs Modify there, as a person would.

get.description:
Search the repository for an application, or for the company's AI in the name of a person.

The same search the page does - customers, folders, registered documents and file names - answered
for the AD account behind the call: the key's own account, or, with a ticket, the person who asked.
Nothing is in the answer that that account may not see.
